content: Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. We've got about 45 minutes together, and we're going to be talking about your food choices and opinions. It'll be recorded for research purposes, so just a heads up on that. The main thing to know is that there are genuinely no right or wrong answers here — I'm not looking for anything in particular, I just want to hear what you actually think and what your actual experiences are. So try not to overthink things, just speak freely. And this is meant to feel more like a conversation than an interview — you don't have to take turns or wait to be asked, just jump in if something connects with what someone else is saying or if you've got something to add. The only thing I'd ask is that you're respectful of each other and try to keep individual answers reasonably brief so everyone gets a chance to speak. Okay, let's get going — let's start by going around and saying your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.
I'm Amir, I'm from Birmingham. West Midlands. Twenty years old.

Yeah, I'm Ibrahim. I'm from the North East, urban area. I'm twenty-four. 

*pauses slightly*

Good to meet you all.
Right, I'm Isaiah. I'm from Leeds, so Yorkshire and the Humber. I'm twenty-six. Good to meet you lot as well.
Right, I'm Will. I'm from rural Scotland — quite a bit more quiet than what you lot are used to, I reckon. I'm twenty-nine. Good to meet you all too.
Right, I'm David. I'm from urban Scotland — Edinburgh area, so yeah, not quite as quiet as Will's patch. I'm twenty-seven. Good to meet everyone.

Great, good to have everyone here — Amir, Ibrahim, Isaiah, Will, and David. Right, let's get into it. I want to start with something fairly easy and specific. Think about where you tend to spend time with your male friends — could be a particular pub, a park, a gym, wherever it is for you. What's your favourite place in your city or area to hang out with the lads, and what is it about that place that makes it work for you?

There's this spot near the quayside — you know, down by the river. It's got a few bars and restaurants around it, pretty lively on weekends. We usually end up at one of the pubs there, nothing fancy. I think it just works because it's central, easy to get to, and there's always something going on — live music sometimes, people about. You can grab a drink, have a laugh, doesn't matter if you're there for two hours or five. And honestly, the food's decent too if you're hungry — they do good burgers, steaks, that kind of thing. That matters when you've had a few and want something substantial, you know?

Yeah, that makes sense. We've got similar spots around Birmingham — like the Bullring's got that vibe, loads going on, but honestly I'm more into the quieter places. Cannon Hill Park's where we actually hang out proper, you know? It's not just about getting drinks and that. Like, you can actually have a conversation without shouting over everyone. And yeah, the food thing Ibrahim mentioned — I get that. When you're hungry you want something decent, a proper meal. But I think for me it's more about just being able to chill and actually talk to your mates rather than just being in a mad busy spot. Nothing against it, just depends what you're in the mood for.

Yeah, I hear you on that. Cannon Hill sounds good for that. But I think the quayside's got both, to be honest. Like, yeah, it gets busy and there's energy, but it's not chaotic — you can still sit down, have proper conversations. It's not like you're forced to be shouting at each other. And that's kind of the point of it for us, I think. You've got the option, you know? Some nights you want that buzz going on around you, other nights you just want to chill with a pint and talk about stuff. The fact that it's got the food, the bars, the space to actually sit and be with your mates — that's why it works. You don't have to choose between one thing or the other.

Fair point, yeah. I suppose I was thinking more like chaotic busy, but you're right — having options is the thing, isn't it? You can pick how you want the night to go depending on what you're after. Cannon Hill's quieter so it's naturally more that way, but what you're saying about having the buzz there if you want it but also being able to chat properly... that does work. I get that. You get the flexibility, basically.

Yeah, that flexibility thing — that's the bit that's different where I am, really. Like, there's maybe one or two pubs that work, and that's kind of it. You go there because it's the only option, not because you're choosing between a few different vibes, you know? You can't just decide halfway through the night "oh, I fancy somewhere quieter" or "let's go find a spot with a bit more going on." It's what you've got.

Don't get me wrong, it's alright. The people are good, everyone knows everyone. But there's no flexibility about it. You're not picking how the night's going to feel — the place kind of determines it for you. Whereas what you two are saying, it sounds like you've actually got... options. You can tailor what you're doing depending on what you want. That's a different thing entirely.

That's a really different picture, Will — having the place make the decision for you rather than the other way round. David, Isaiah, we haven't heard from you two yet — whereabouts do you tend to end up with your mates?

Yeah, so I'm similar to Will in some ways, I think. I mean, Edinburgh's got loads going on, so it's not quite the same constraint he's talking about, but... I don't know, I'm not really one for planning it out that much. I tend to just end up at the same few spots, if I'm honest. There's a couple of pubs near Leith Walk that mates and I gravitate towards, and we just kind of go there because we know it, not necessarily because we've weighed up all the options, you know? 

Will's right though — there's something about having choice and then there's something about just... knowing where you're going. I think both have their thing. Like, the spots we go to aren't fancy, they're just familiar. You know the people behind the bar, you know roughly what you're getting. And that works fine for just hanging out and having a laugh with the lads.

But yeah, I do have more options than Will's describing, so I guess if I got bored of Leith Walk I could try somewhere else. Whereas if you've only got the one or two places, that's... that's just the reality of where you live, isn't it?

Right, yeah — that's fair. You've got the option there if you want it, even if you don't always use it. That's different from what I'm saying. Like, you could get bored and go somewhere new if you fancied it. I can't really do that.

And I'm not saying familiarity's bad — that bit David said about knowing the people behind the bar and what you're getting, that's exactly it for me too. That's comfortable. But it's not the same as choosing to be familiar with a place because you like it, you know? It's more just... this is where everyone goes because it's the only place that works. You're not weighing it up. There's no "well, I could go somewhere else" sitting in the back of your head, even if you don't act on it.
Isaiah, we haven't heard from you yet — whereabouts do you end up with your mates in Leeds?

Yeah, so I'm a bit like David, I reckon. There's this spot — couple of bars and a gym actually near where I live, so we end up there a lot just because it's easy, you know? It's not really a conscious choice most of the time, just... that's where we go. But I think what you're all saying about having options — I get that. Leeds has got loads of places, so like, if we got bored we could go somewhere else, but we just don't really bother most of the time.

I think the familiar thing is... it's comfortable, isn't it? You know what you're getting, you're not arsed with trying somewhere new every time you want to hang out. But Will's point about only having one or two places — that does sound different. Like, at least I've got the option there if I wanted it, even if I don't think about it much.

And yeah, the food thing — we usually grab something while we're there or after. It's not like we're planning a meal out or anything, just whatever's available and decent. Does the job.

Cheers Isaiah. So we've got a few different pictures there — from lively spots with loads going on, to quieter places, to just ending up where's familiar, to genuinely not having much choice at all. Interesting how that varies. Let's shift to something connected — thinking about your day-to-day now, how do you actually decide what to eat? Like, what's driving that for you?

Honestly? I don't really decide much. I just... eat meat. That's what I do. I'll have chicken a few times a week, fish quite a bit, red meat when I fancy it. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking about it — it's just what I reach for, what feels normal. 

I mean, I'll eat what's there, innit? If someone's cooking, I'll have what they've made. But if I'm just getting something myself, it's usually got meat in it because that's... that's just what I eat. I don't really think past that. It's not a big decision or anything, just how I eat.

I get what you're saying, but I think for me it's a bit different. Like, yeah, meat's what I eat — chicken pretty much every day, red meat couple times a week, fish — but it's not just like I'm not thinking about it, you know? I do choose it. It's not just defaulting to whatever's there. 

I mean, it feels normal and comfortable, yeah, that bit's true. But it's more like... I actively want it. It's satisfying, and I know what I'm getting. That's different from just not thinking about it and grabbing whatever, innit? 

I suppose for me it's somewhere in between what Isaiah's saying and the familiar thing David was talking about with the pubs. It's familiar and comfortable, but it's also a choice I'm making, not just something that happens because I'm not paying attention.

Yeah, fair point actually. I think I was underselling it a bit. I do prefer it, you know? It's not just like I'm mindlessly grabbing it. When I think about what I want to eat, meat's what comes to mind. It's satisfying — fills you up properly. I'd miss it if I wasn't eating it.

So yeah, maybe it's more like what you're saying, Amir. It's familiar and comfortable, but it's also that I actually want it. Not just defaulting because I can't be bothered to think about alternatives or whatever. I genuinely prefer it to... I don't know, the other options.

Yeah, that's more it, I think. But even then — I mean, when you say you prefer it, is that because you've actually thought about what else is out there? Or is it more like... you prefer it because that's what you've always had, so anything else just doesn't feel right?

Like for me, I know there's other stuff — vegetarian stuff, whatever — but I genuinely don't want it. And maybe part of that is just because that's how I grew up, meat's just what we ate. But it's not like I haven't considered it, you know? I've seen people do it, I know it exists. I just... I wouldn't want to eat like that. That's different from just not thinking about alternatives at all.

Nah, you're right actually. I haven't really... considered it, not properly anyway. Like, I know vegetarian stuff exists, obviously, but I haven't sat down and thought about it or tried it or anything like that. It's just not something I do.

I think for me it's more just... that's what I eat, that's what's normal. I don't really have a strong feeling about it either way, to be honest. It's not like I'm actively rejecting alternatives or anything — I just don't think about them. Whereas what you're saying, you've actually weighed it up and decided nah, not for me. That's different, innit? I'm just kind of... not engaging with the question at all, really.

Isaiah, that's an interesting distinction you've just drawn — between actively weighing something up and deciding against it, versus just... not really bringing it into the picture at all. Does that resonate with how any of you others think about your food choices? Will, Ibrahim, David — what's it like for you?

Yeah, I think... I'm a bit like Isaiah, to be honest. Not in a bad way, just — I eat meat, I eat dairy, that's what I do. I don't really sit around thinking about it. It's just what's there, what I've always had.

But what Isaiah said at the end there — about not engaging with the question — that's kind of it for me too. I'm not actively going, "right, I've considered being vegetarian and decided against it." It's more like... it's just not something I think about. It's normal to eat how I eat. 

Though I suppose the difference with me and the pub thing we were talking about earlier — with the familiar spots in Edinburgh and Leeds, you've both got other options sitting there even if you don't use them. With food, it's a bit like my situation with the pubs. There's no real alternative framework there, you know? It's just how you eat. It's not that I'm choosing meat over something else — it's more that the "something else" doesn't really... exist as an option in your head. It's not a conscious decision at all.

Yeah, but I think — I mean, Will's right about the alternative not really being there mentally, but I don't think that's the same as me not having considered it, you know? Like, I know vegetarians exist. I've definitely seen people eat vegetarian stuff. It's not like it's invisible or something.

I think the difference is more just... I don't need to consider it, because I know what I want. It's not like I'm avoiding the question or I haven't thought about it because I'm not capable of thinking about it. It's more that when I think about what I want to eat, meat's just the answer. I don't need to weigh it up against something else because I already know.

Maybe that sounds like splitting hairs after what I said before, but it does feel different to me. It's not that alternatives don't exist as a mental option — they exist, I just don't need them. That's a choice, innit? Even if it's not a super conscious one.

I hear what you're saying, but I'm not sure that's quite right though. Like — knowing vegetarians exist is different from actually considering it as something for you, yeah? 

It's a bit like... I know there's loads of pubs in Edinburgh. I know they exist. But that doesn't mean I'm actually considering going to them as an option for how I spend my time. That's not a choice I'm making — it's just not part of my frame of reference because I don't have access to it in the same way you lot do.

And I think that's what we're saying with food too. You knowing vegetarians exist doesn't mean you've actually weighed it up as something you could do. It's just... background noise, isn't it? It's not like you're going "right, meat or no meat" and picking meat. You're just eating meat because that's what you eat. That's not choosing meat over vegetarian — that's not engaging with the choice at all.

I don't think it's a choice just because the alternative technically exists somewhere in the world. It's only a choice if you're actually considering it as something you could do yourself.

Yeah, okay. Fair enough. I think you're right actually. I was trying to have it both ways there, wasn't I?

Like, I don't actually consider it for myself. I know it exists, but I'm not sitting there thinking "could I do that?" It's not like I'm weighing it up and going nah, not for me. I'm just... not thinking about it at all. It's not part of how I think about what I eat.

So yeah, you're right — that's different from choosing. It's more just what I do, and I don't really bring alternatives into it. I was making it sound more deliberate than it actually is, I reckon.
David, we haven't heard from you on this one yet — when you think about what you eat day to day, does any of that land for you?

Yeah, I think... I mean, I eat meat, obviously, but it's not really a big thing for me either way, to be honest. It's just what I have. Chicken, bit of red meat, fish sometimes. But I don't feel strongly about it, you know? Like, I'm not sitting there thinking "I really want meat" or making some conscious choice about it. It's just... that's what's there, that's what I eat.

But I think where I'd maybe push back a bit on what's been said — I don't know if it has to be this big thing about choosing or not choosing. Like, yeah, I'm not actively weighing up vegetarian options every time I make dinner, but that doesn't mean I'm not... aware of it? I know people who don't eat meat. I know it's a thing. And I just... it's not for me. Not because I've sat down and done some big analysis, but because it's not something I want to do.

I think there's maybe a difference between "I haven't considered it" and "I've kind of considered it exists, I just don't care about it." For me it's more the second one. It's not like alternatives are invisible — they're just not particularly relevant to how I eat, if that makes sense. I'm not choosing meat *over* something else. I'm just eating how I eat.
Ibrahim, we haven't heard from you yet on this — when you think about what you eat day to day, where does that land for you?

I think I'm somewhere in the middle of what you lot have been saying, to be honest. Like, I eat meat — red meat couple times a week, chicken, fish, that kind of thing. And yeah, it's normal for me, it's what I've grown up with. But I don't feel that strongly attached to it, you know? It's not like I'm going around thinking "I really need my meat" or anything. It's just... that's what I eat.

But I also know vegetarians exist, I know people who do it. It's not invisible or anything. I'm just... not that bothered either way. It doesn't feel like a big choice to me. I'm not sitting there weighing it up — meat or no meat. It's more like it doesn't matter that much to me. If there was vegetarian food there, I'd probably eat it. If there's meat, I'll eat that. It's not something I've got strong feelings about.

So I guess for me it's not really about choosing meat so much as just... not really thinking about food choices at all, if that makes sense. It's not a thing for me either way.

Thanks Ibrahim. So across the five of you there's a real range there — from actively wanting meat and knowing why, to it just not being something that crosses your mind. That's useful to have on the table. Let me move us on to something a bit more specific. Do you think your gender influences what you eat? And why — or why not?

Yeah, I think it does, to be honest. Like, growing up in Birmingham, there's definitely a thing about meat and being a bloke, you know? Like, a proper meal is meat — that's just how it was. You have your chicken, your steak, whatever. That's what makes it a real meal, not like... I don't know, salad or whatever people think vegetarian stuff is.

I'm not saying I think about it consciously every time I eat or anything, but it's definitely shaped how I think about food. Like, meat feels masculine, feels normal in a way that... other stuff doesn't. I can see how that comes from growing up in that culture, seeing my dad eating meat, seeing that as just what you do as a man.

But I dunno, I'm also not sure how much I actually believe all that, if I'm being honest. Like, I do want meat because it's satisfying and I enjoy it — that's real. But I can't tell if that's genuine preference or if it's just what I've been taught to prefer, you know? It's hard to separate the two sometimes.

Amir's putting his finger on something interesting there — that question of whether you genuinely prefer meat or whether you've just been taught to prefer it, and whether you can even tell the difference. Does that land for anyone else? Does that distinction feel real to you, or does it look different from where you're sitting?

Yeah, I think what you're saying — that's actually... yeah. I've been saying it's not a big deal for me, food choices and that, but hearing you say it like that makes me think I'm maybe just not paying attention to it properly, you know?

Like, I grew up here in the North East, and meat's definitely just what you do. My dad ate meat, my mum cooked meat — that's just normal. And I've never really questioned it. But I don't know if that's the same as what you're describing or if it's different. Like, I'm genuinely not sure if I prefer meat because I actually like it, or if I prefer it because that's what I've been taught is normal, is what a bloke does.

I can't really tell the difference, to be honest. It's just so much part of how I think about eating that I can't separate it out. Is that the same thing as you're saying — that you can't tell if it's genuine preference or what you've been conditioned to prefer? Or is it different because I'm actually not even thinking about it enough to have that question in the first place?

I don't know. I think maybe I'm just... less aware of it than you are, Amir. But hearing you put it like that, I'm not sure that's a good thing.

I don't know, mate. I mean... yeah, maybe you're less aware of it, but I'm not sure that makes it worse or anything. Like, at least you're not sitting there going round in circles about it like I am.

But I think there's something different, innit? Like, you're saying you can't tell the difference because you've never really thought about it. And I get that. But for me, it's more like — I have thought about it, I know there's alternatives, and I still want meat. So I'm more confident about it, I guess? But then the question is whether I'm confident because I've actually made a choice, or whether I'm just more aware of the conditioning without being able to do anything about it.

I think... I'd probably miss meat if it wasn't there, you know? That feels like a genuine preference to me. But whether that's because I actually like it or because I've been brought up thinking that's what I'm supposed to want — that's the bit I can't figure out. And honestly, I'm not sure it matters that much either. Like, at the end of the day, do you need to have tested every alternative to know what you actually prefer? Probably not.

Yeah, but I think that's different though, innit? Like, you've actually made a choice. You've thought about it, you know alternatives exist, and you've gone "nah, I want meat." That's a decision you've made, even if you can't fully untangle where it comes from.

What I'm realizing is — I haven't really done that. I'm not going "I prefer meat," I'm just... eating it because it's there. I haven't tested anything else, I haven't thought about it properly. It's not like I've weighed it up and decided. I'm just drifting, you know?

And I think that's different from what you're saying. You feel like you'd miss meat if it wasn't there — that sounds like an actual preference to me. Whereas me, I couldn't tell you if I'd miss it because I've never even thought about what the alternative would feel like. That's not the same as knowing what you prefer and sticking with it.

I don't know though, Ibrahim. Like, you're saying I've made a choice because I've thought about it, but... have I really? I mean, I know vegetarians exist, yeah, but I've never actually sat down and tried it, properly tried it, you know? I've just decided it's not for me without really testing it.

So is that actually different from what you're doing? Like, you're drifting because you haven't thought about it. But me — I might just be drifting in a different direction because I've decided ahead of time it's not something I'd want. I haven't actually tested the alternative any more than you have, I've just made it sound more deliberate by thinking about why I don't want it.

I mean, I probably wouldn't want to eat vegetarian anyway. That's a real thing for me. But I'm not sure I can say I've properly chosen meat over it when I haven't actually... you know, experienced both properly. That's just picking a lane early and then convincing myself it was a choice, innit?

Fair point, yeah. I think you're right actually. We're probably both just... doing the same thing, just thinking about it differently. You've thought about it enough to go "nah, not for me," and I haven't thought about it at all. But neither of us has actually tested it, so maybe that's not as different as I was making it sound.

Like, we're both just eating meat because that's what we do. You've got reasons for why you don't want anything else, I haven't even got to that point. But at the end of the day, we're in the same place, aren't we? Just eating what we eat.

I think maybe I was overthinking it a bit. Like, I was making it sound like you'd made some proper deliberate choice and I was just drifting. But you're saying you haven't really tested the alternative either, so... yeah, maybe we're both just drifting, just in slightly different ways. You're drifting while thinking about it, I'm drifting while not thinking about it.

Ibrahim's just landed on something — 'we're both drifting, just thinking about it differently.' Does that resonate with anyone else, or does it look different from where you're sitting? Will, Isaiah — you've been quiet on this one.

Actually, wait — I'm not sure "drifting" is even the right word for what I'm doing, you know? Like, I keep saying that, but I'm actively choosing meat every time I eat. That's not drifting, is it? That's just a choice I'm making, and maybe I've been calling it drifting because it sounds less... I dunno, less like I've actually decided something.

Because I have decided it. I eat meat. I choose it. I'm not floating along passively — I'm picking that option every single time. So why am I framing it like something's just happening to me?

I think maybe it's easier to say "oh, I'm just drifting, it's what I grew up with" than to go "yeah, I'm choosing this." Even if the choice isn't super thought-through, it's still a choice I'm making.

So Ibrahim's just pulled the rug out from under the 'drifting' framing — saying actually, no, I'm making a choice every time, I just find it easier to call it drifting. Will, Isaiah — that's the question on the table now: is it a choice, is it drift, or is that distinction even real?

I think Ibrahim's... I don't know, he's kind of having it both ways there, isn't he?

Like, he's saying he's actively choosing meat every time, but that's not really what he said earlier. He said he doesn't think about it, he just eats it because it's there. And now he's calling that a choice because... what, because he's the one putting the fork in his mouth? That's not the same thing.

A choice is when you've actually considered something. When the alternative is real in your head as something you could do. Ibrahim just admitted he hasn't done that — he's never sat down and thought about it, never tested it. So saying "I'm choosing meat" is kind of... it's reframing it to make it sound more deliberate than it is.

It's like what I was saying earlier about the pubs. Just because I'm the one walking into the pub doesn't mean I'm choosing it over somewhere else if there isn't anywhere else to choose from, you know? It's just what happens. That's not a choice.

I think Ibrahim's just feeling a bit uncomfortable with the word "drifting" because it sounds passive, but the thing is — it kind of is passive. That doesn't mean it's bad or anything, it's just what it is. Calling it a choice doesn't make it more deliberate if you haven't actually considered the alternative.

Yeah, okay. Fair enough. You're right, I was doing that — trying to have it both ways. Like, I don't think about it, but then I'm calling it a choice to make myself feel better about it or something.

I think what happened is... hearing you lot talk about it made me uncomfortable with just saying "I drift" because that sounds like I'm not responsible for it or something. But Will's right — that's not what choosing actually means. Choosing means you've thought about the alternative and gone one way or the other. I haven't done that.

So yeah, I'm not choosing meat. I'm just eating it because it's what I do, because it's normal, because that's how I was brought up. And I haven't really sat with what that means, if I'm honest. I've just been eating it without thinking about it, and when the conversation starts asking me to think about it, I try to dress it up as a choice to avoid looking like I'm just... mindlessly following what I grew up with.

That's probably not great to admit, but Will's calling me out on the dodgy reasoning, so.

So the group's landed somewhere interesting — this idea that what feels like choice is actually habit that's been given a more deliberate-sounding name. Ibrahim, Amir, Will — you've all circled around that. But here's what I'm not quite hearing yet: what's doing the conditioning? Because Amir mentioned right at the start — meat feels masculine, watching his dad, a proper meal is a meat meal. If it's not really a choice, is gender part of what's shaping the default? Isaiah, David — does that land for you, or does it look different from where you're sitting?

Yeah, I mean — that's the thing I was trying to say earlier, isn't it? Like, yeah, there's definitely a gender thing. Growing up, meat was masculine. That's just how it was framed. My dad ate meat, a proper meal had meat in it. You don't question it when you're a kid, it's just normal.

But when the moderator's asking it like that — is gender shaping the default — I don't know if I can honestly say it is for me, because I can't separate it out anymore. Like, I don't know if I actually prefer meat because I genuinely like it, or if I prefer it because I've been taught that's what I'm supposed to prefer as a bloke. And hearing Ibrahim say all that stuff about drifting and then calling it a choice — I'm kind of recognizing I might be doing the same thing, you know? Like, I've convinced myself I've made a deliberate choice, but maybe I'm just... I've grown up thinking meat is what you do, and now I'm defending it like it's something I've actually decided on.

So yeah, I think gender's definitely in there. Whether it's the whole thing or just part of it — I can't really tell anymore. But it's definitely part of how I think about eating meat, like it or not.

So there's a lot of agreement building here — gender's in the mix, the conditioning's real, but it's all murky and hard to untangle. I want to push on that a bit, because I'm not sure it's always as hard to see as you're all making it sound. Think about a concrete moment — not the abstract question of whether gender shapes your preferences, but something more specific: if one of your male friends ordered a salad, or said he'd gone vegetarian, would that register? Would it land differently than if he'd ordered a burger? Isaiah, David — you've been sitting with this. What do you actually think?

Yeah, it would register differently, to be honest. Like, if a mate ordered a salad... I don't know, there'd be something there, wouldn't there? A bit of a double take, maybe. Not in like a massive aggressive way, but it would be... noticeable.

And I think that's the thing that's been bugging me a bit listening to everyone talk about this — like, we're all sitting here going "oh, I just eat meat, it's not a big deal, gender doesn't really factor in," but then if someone actually stepped outside that, it would feel weird. That's the bit that tells you something's going on, innit?

Like, if it genuinely didn't matter, if it was just a neutral preference thing, then a mate ordering a salad would be the same as ordering a burger. But it's not. There's definitely a... I don't know, a feeling there. And I think that feeling is kind of the point. That's where the gender stuff is actually living, even if we don't think about it consciously.

So no, I don't buy the idea that I've just made some free choice about what I eat and gender's got nothing to do with it. Because the fact that a mate doing something different would register — that's evidence that there's a norm there. And norms come from somewhere. They come from exactly what Amir was talking about — growing up seeing men do one thing, and that becomes what feels normal, what feels right.
